chats.title: how does the memory bench work

messages.text: how does the memory bench work

The benchmark holds everything fixed except the memory system: each system answers the same questions with the same answering agent, and the same grader scores every answer.

**Procedure**

1. **Ingestion.** Each system reads the full haystack (the chat history or event stream) through its normal ingestion path and builds its store. Tophat starts from an empty store for every question; the live store is never opened.
2. **Answering.** A single answering agent, with a fixed model and loop, is used for every system: up to 8 tool calls (search, plus read where the system exposes it), then an answer. Score differences therefore reflect retrieval, not prompting or model choice.
3. **Grading.** A separate model labels each answer correct or incorrect. On LongMemEval it uses the benchmark's official judge prompts verbatim.
4. **Ceiling.** An "all in context" condition places the entire haystack in the prompt with no memory system, which bounds what the answering model can achieve when nothing is lost.

**Question sets**

- **2a:** the 15 hardest questions in LongMemEval-S, a public benchmark with about 115k tokens of chat history per question. Selection was fixed before any system ran, taking the questions published systems most often miss, stratified across all seven question types.
- **2b:** 99 questions over one person's real traces (messages, workouts, sleep and code history), embedded in 7,326 events (about 300k tokens).
why should i trust the numbers

**Controls**

- **Pre-registered selection.** 2a questions were chosen by a seeded rule over other groups' published results, before any tophat run.
- **Fixed answering and grading.** The answering model, loop and grader are identical across systems; official judge prompts are used where they exist.
- **Leakage.** Tool results never indicate which sessions contain the answer, and each question gets a fresh store.
- **Records.** Every row keeps the answer, the judge's label, the full tool trace and the per-question cost. Each harness bug found during the runs is logged together with what was re-run.
- **Baselines at defaults.** Mem0, Zep/Graphiti, Letta, agentmemory and Supermemory run on their own default configurations; any deviation (for example local embeddings where the default requires an OpenAI key) is recorded beside the result.

**Limitations**

- **Sample size.** 2a has 15 questions, so one question is about 7 points. Differences of one or two questions are within noise; repeated runs of the same system varied by one question.
- **2b covers one person.** The questions come from real traces, not synthetic dialogue, but from a single person's data, so they show how systems handle one real history and do not establish how results vary across people.
- **Model grader.** The judge occasionally mislabels answers, mostly on preference questions and answers open to dispute.
- **Retrieval mode.** Tophat's embedding search was disabled in every run; all tophat figures are full-text-search only.
how does sharing work

Short version: a scope is a group that controls who can read a row. The hub holds only ciphertext and routing metadata, and a note reaches someone when it is written into or shared to a scope they belong to and both sides sync. I'll check the repo notes to confirm the details.

**Scopes and groups.** A scope is a group that controls who can read a row. Every note, entity and work item carries the scopes allowed to read it, and you can read a row if any of its scopes is one of yours. Members have a role in a scope: read, write or admin. Anything you write without naming a scope stays in your private scope.

**What the hub can see.** The hub only relays ciphertext. It stores the sealed log plus routing metadata: device and user ids, group ids and memberships. It never holds a scope key, so it cannot read notes, search them or build pages. It is append-only, with no delete route. The caveat is trust in the operator: whoever runs the hub issues device tokens, so if that matters, run your own hub.

**How a note reaches someone.**
1. You write the note into a scope, or widen an existing one with `tophat-linknotes share note <id> alex,<scope>`.
2. The note is sealed with a fresh key, and that key is wrapped to each scope key allowed to read it.
3. Your next `sync` pushes the ciphertext to the hub.
4. The other person's replica syncs, receives the scope's key for its device and sees the note.

To take it back, run `tophat-linknotes retract note <id>`. The log keeps the record, but replicas hide it.

**Joining a shared scope.** The hub operator gives you a device token. You `init` with it and `sync` to register your device key. The scope's admin runs `scope add <scope> <user> write` and syncs, then you sync again to receive the rows.

chats.title: how is tophat different from other assistants

messages.text: how is tophat different from other assistants

A few ways:

- **Open source.** All the code is yours to read, change and run.
- **It runs on your own machine,** so it can use your apps directly (Messages, Contacts, Photos, Find My, your browser) and act as you, not through a cloud integration.
- **Better memory.** It keeps a growing graph of who and what matters to you, built from your mail, messages, notes and chats, and it cites where each fact came from.
- **It aims to capture all your context.** Most assistants know what you told them in one chat. Tophat tries to know everything, so that over time it can act as you rather than just answer questions for you.
how does tophat make money

It doesn't. Tophat is supported by donations.

The code is open, and the core has no dependencies beyond Node itself, so you can use it as a base and customize it however you like: fork it, strip it down, or build your own assistant on top of it.

chats.title: where does my data go with tophat

messages.text: where does my data go with tophat

Your memory lives in a local SQLite file on your machine. Nothing is uploaded to us.

The one thing that leaves your machine is what goes to your model provider: each turn sends the relevant context to the model you configured (Anthropic by default, or a local model if you plug one in).

Sharing with other people is optional and off by default. When you turn it on, rows are end-to-end encrypted per group, and the relay in between only ever holds ciphertext.

chats.title: what do i need to run tophat

messages.text: what do i need to run tophat

A Mac (Linux works too, with fewer app integrations), Node, and a model API key (Anthropic by default).

A dedicated Mac is nice, since tophat can then use the apps and stay on all day, but your everyday Mac works as well.

To install, paste the repo link into a coding agent like Claude Code or Codex and ask it to check the code and set it up.
shld i switch to dumbbell bench? smt smt stability

Probably yes, but which goal goes first is your call. Here is what I'm going on.

**Your barbell bench, Day A, from your hevy log:**

| day | working sets |
|---|---|
| Oct 20 | 5 at 90 lb, then 5 and 5 at 85 |
| Oct 24 | 5 at 90, then 6 and 6 at 85 |
| Oct 30 | 3 sets of 5 at 90 ("full 90s!") |
| Nov 5 | 6, 5, 4 at 90 |

**Your goals:** you told your friend J on Nov 5 that benching your own weight is "almost there", and on Nov 10 you said the bigger goal is physical ability, being able to frolic, and staying uninjured for a long time.

**Stability:** it comes up in your notes more than once. You wrote "we need stabs lol" on Sep 27, asked on Oct 20 (leg curl) whether your left leg is stronger than your right, and on Nov 5 wrote that you need to work on knee stability at the bottom of the squat. Your left side is the weaker one.

So I think yes, for the longer goal. Dumbbells give each arm its own path, so the weak side can't hide behind the strong one. That is useful, because once the gap shows up you can train it.

The cost is the other goal. You'd leave a barbell progression that is moving right now, and dumbbell bench usually lands around 35 to 40% of the barbell weight per hand (s: recall), so roughly 30 to 35 lb each. If the bodyweight bench is a few jumps away, I'd finish that first and switch the slot after. If you'd rather start finding the left-right gap now, switch now and don't feel bad about the number dropping.

You also said you aren't adding sets. A swap is one for one, so nothing else in the day changes.
ok which one would u do

Hit the bench goal first. You're at 6, 5, 4 at 90, and the last time you got a clean 3x5 at 90 was Oct 30, so the bodyweight bench is probably a few jumps away. Then swap the barbell bench for dumbbell bench in the same slot and start around 30 lb per hand for 3 sets of 8.

If a session ever feels sketchy on the bar before then (you wrote about a shaky third set on Sep 19), that's the day to swap early.
how do i work up to a pistol squat

You're already partway, so here is where your log puts you.

**What you've done (hevy):** on Oct 24 you did 3x8 pistols to a stack of blocks, with a note to start high, do touch-down squats, sweep the free leg forward at the end, then lower the blocks. On Nov 5 it was 2x6 and then 3 reps. If you lowered the blocks that week, a drop in reps is expected; the log doesn't say.

**What's limiting you:** probably not strength. You squatted 6, 6, 7 at 145 lb the same day. Your own notes name the limit: knee stability, range of motion and holding at the bottom on Nov 5, and "hold at bottom to stabilize" on Oct 24. Your left leg is also the one you've flagged as weaker, on the leg curl and the split squats.

**So I'd do this:**
1. **Keep the block progression.** Lower the stack only when every set is clean, as you already planned.
2. **Pause at the bottom.** Two to three seconds, every rep, on the blocks. That is the stability work.
3. **Left leg first.** Do the weaker side first and match the right to its reps.
4. **Eccentric negatives** once the blocks are low: lower for 3 to 5 seconds, then stand up with both legs.
5. **A light counterweight** (5 to 10 lb held out in front) makes the last steps easier. Drop it when the free pistol is close.
6. **Ankles.** If your heel lifts at the bottom, put a small plate under it for now, and work the wall knee-over-toe drill before the set.

Keep it to the slot you already have on Day A; 2 or 3 sets of 3 to 5 per leg is enough.
i want to play with light more in my sketches, how do i do a value study

A value study is a small, fast sketch that skips line and detail and only works out where the light and dark go. Painters do them to settle the light before they commit to a drawing.

- **Go small.** About 2 by 3 inches, 5 to 10 minutes each. Small keeps you from drawing details.
- **Use three values.** Paper white for the lights, one mid gray, one dark. Squint at the scene until it falls into those three shapes, then block them in flat.
- **Pick the light first.** Decide where it comes from and where the lightest light meets the darkest dark. That edge is where the eye goes.
- **Do a few of the same scene.** Move the light or the darks around and see which one still reads from across the room.

A soft pencil (4B to 6B) or a gray brush pen works; one gray marker plus a black one is fastest.
why only three values?

Because the eye reads a picture as a few big shapes of light and dark before anything else. Three forces you to decide which areas group together; with ten you end up copying every shift you see and the light gets muddy. Once three works, add a fourth for the half-tones and stop there.

chats.title: encyclopedia cave, what was that place

messages.text: my friend brought me to encyclopedia cave that was crazy what was that place so cool

That's Encyclopedia Cave, the hidden cave near the Stanford Dish. You went on the night of Tue Dec 12, 2023 (s: message): your friend had the group meet at the Dish parking lot around 10:10 pm and at the cave itself around 10:20, and said "Today is for stars". At 1:47 am you texted "Thanks for the great night!" You still have the people from that trip saved together in your contacts under one label.

What it is, from public sources (s: web): a Stanford-hosted photo gallery called "Encyclopedia Cave" ([web.stanford.edu/~siegelr/stanford/encyclopediacave.html](https://web.stanford.edu/~siegelr/stanford/encyclopediacave.html)) from three visits across two years. The captions mention a library, equations, studying in caves, a copy of Origin of Species and a line from Lovecraft left in the cave, so it reads like a study spot people stock with books and notes. A 2023 r/stanford post says the rumor is a cave "somewhere on the dish near the quarry" and that the poster's group couldn't find it.

I couldn't find an official page, so I don't know who looks after it or whether going in is allowed. It's easy to miss, so go with someone who knows the way, like your friend did.
